analysis.one_liner: Taxes foreign owners 1% of property value when U.S. homes sit empty nearly year-round.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House in December 2022 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, but never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 1% annual tax on the estimated value of any U.S. home — a house, condo, or small building of up to four units — owned by a foreign person and occupied as a residence for fewer than 29 days a year. The idea is to make it more expensive to hold American homes as empty investments and push them back into use by people who live in them. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary homebuyers and renters in markets where foreign-owned, vacant homes have taken units off the market; a tax on empty foreign-owned homes creates pressure to sell or rent them out. Federal revenue from the tax would go to the Treasury [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 1% annual excise tax on the estimated value of any U.S. residential property owned by a foreign person and occupied as a dwelling for fewer than 29 days in the year [S2][S3].
Defines covered property broadly to include single-family homes, condos, rowhouses, and buildings of up to four units, plus the land conveyed with them [S2][S3].
Uses the larger of the local property-tax appraisal or the most recent sale price as the value base, so the tax tracks what the property is actually worth [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign persons who own underutilized U.S. homes, roughly 1% of each property's value per year it sits mostly empty [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Foreign owners of vacant U.S. homes

drawbacks.text: A foreign owner who personally uses the home for 29 or more days a year — for example, as a part-time vacation home — owes nothing, so the bill leaves that pattern untouched [S3].
The bill does nothing about vacant or investment homes owned by U.S. persons or U.S.-based investors, which are a larger part of the vacancy problem [S3].
A 1% annual charge is small next to typical home-price appreciation, so it may not be enough on its own to change investor behavior in the hottest markets [S3].
Counting days of occupancy is difficult to verify and enforce, and the bill provides little detail on how occupancy would be checked [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at a real and widely felt problem — homes held empty by overseas owners while local buyers compete for scarce housing — and its targeted tax is a reasonable tool for it. But it is narrow: it spares foreign owners who visit 29 days a year, does nothing about domestic investors holding empty homes, and a 1% charge may be too small to force sales in fast-appreciating markets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs introduced the bill on December 6, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, where it received no further action [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign owners of underutilized American homes keep holding them tax-free under this approach, and no alternative version advanced either.

for.name: Rep. Chris Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Chair Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill for committee action during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a lone Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and never advanced far enough for a party-line vote to take shape [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Foreign owners of U.S. residential property
industries.note: The bill taxes foreign holders of homes that sit empty almost all year at 1% of the property's value annually, directly targeting the practice of holding American housing as an idle store of wealth. Its interest in avoiding the tax runs against local buyers and renters looking for homes.
A tax on idle foreign-held homes could push more units onto the sale or rental market, which would ease prices for local buyers, though the effect depends on how many homes this actually frees up.
